name: Pho
description: Rice noodle soup in a clear beef broth simmered with spices, topped with sliced beef or chicken (phở gà). It emerged in Nam Định province in northern Vietnam in the early 20th century and is now eaten nationwide.
how_to_eat: Add lime, chilli and herbs to taste, and eat with chopsticks and a spoon.
how_to_order: Ask for 'phở bò' (beef) or 'phở gà' (chicken), usually as breakfast.

name: Bun Cha
description: Grilled pork patties and pork belly served in a sweet-sour fish sauce dip with rice vermicelli and fresh herbs. It is a Hanoi lunchtime classic.
how_to_eat: Dip noodles and herbs into the bowl of pork and sauce.
how_to_order: Look for smoky charcoal grills at lunchtime and ask for 'bún chả'.

name: Cha Ca La Vong
description: Catfish marinated in turmeric, galangal and fermented rice, grilled over charcoal and then finished in a hot pan with dill and spring onions. The Đoàn family opened their Hanoi eatery in 1871, and its street was later renamed Grilled Fish Lane (Phố Chả Cá).
how_to_eat: Eat with rice vermicelli, herbs, peanuts and mắm tôm shrimp sauce.
how_to_order: Ask for 'chả cá' at restaurants on Chả Cá street in Hanoi's Old Quarter.

name: Banh Cuon
description: Thin steamed rice sheets rolled around minced pork and wood ear mushroom, topped with fried shallots. It comes from northern Vietnam and is eaten for breakfast across the country.
how_to_eat: Dip in nước chấm fish sauce with slices of chả lụa pork sausage.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bánh cuốn' at breakfast stalls where the sheets are steamed to order.

name: Bun Rieu
description: Rice vermicelli in a sour tomato and crab broth with a crab paste topping, often with fried tofu. It comes from the Red River Delta and is known throughout Vietnam.
how_to_eat: Add shrimp paste, lime and herbs to taste.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bún riêu cua' (crab) at street stalls.

name: Egg Coffee
description: Robusta coffee topped with a cream of egg yolk whipped with sugar and condensed milk. It was created in Hanoi in the late 1940s, when milk was scarce, by the founder of Café Giảng.
how_to_eat: Stir the foam in gradually or eat it with a spoon first.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cà phê trứng' hot or iced at Old Quarter cafés.

name: Bun Bo Hue
description: A spicy beef and pork noodle soup flavoured with lemongrass and fermented shrimp paste, with thick round rice noodles. It is the signature dish of Huế, the old imperial capital.
how_to_eat: Add lime, chilli and banana blossom from the herb plate.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bún bò Huế' at noodle shops, typically for breakfast.

name: Cao Lau
description: Chewy rice noodles with char siu-style pork, greens, bean sprouts and herbs in a little broth. Local legend says the noodles need water from Hội An's Bá Lễ well, so it is rarely found elsewhere.
how_to_eat: Mix the noodles, pork and herbs together with the small amount of broth.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cao lầu' at Hội An eateries and market stalls.

name: Mi Quang
description: Wide rice noodles with a small amount of rich, turmeric-tinted broth, topped with pork, chicken or shrimp, herbs, peanuts and sesame rice crackers. It is the specialty of Quảng Nam and Đà Nẵng.
how_to_eat: Break the rice cracker over the bowl and mix everything.
how_to_order: Ask for 'mì Quảng' with 'tôm thịt' (shrimp and pork) or 'gà' (chicken).

name: Banh Beo
description: Small steamed savoury rice cakes served in little dishes, topped with dried shrimp, pork crackling and spring onion oil. They are a well-known central Vietnamese snack.
how_to_eat: Drizzle fish sauce over each one and scoop out with a spoon.
how_to_order: Ask for a tray of 'bánh bèo' at Huế snack shops.

name: Com Hen
description: Rice mixed with baby river clams, peanuts, pork crackling, herbs and shrimp paste, served with clam broth. It is a specialty of Huế.
how_to_eat: Mix everything together and sip the clam broth alongside.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cơm hến' at Huế street stalls and markets.

name: Banh Khoai
description: A crispy half-moon pancake made with rice batter and egg yolk, filled with shrimp, pork and bean sprouts. It is Huế's own version of bánh xèo.
how_to_eat: Wrap pieces in herbs and dip in the accompanying sauce.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bánh khoái' at Huế street stalls.

name: Banh Mi
description: A crusty baguette filled with pâté, cold cuts or grilled meat, pickled carrot and daikon, cucumber, coriander and chilli. The baguette came with French colonial rule, and the filled Saigon-style sandwich became a popular street food in the 1950s.
how_to_eat: Eat on the go, straight from the paper wrapper.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bánh mì thịt' (mixed meats) at street carts.

name: Com Tam
description: Broken rice served with a grilled pork chop, steamed pork and egg loaf and shredded pork skin, with sweet fish sauce. It is Saigon's everyday rice plate.
how_to_eat: Pour the fish sauce over the rice and pork.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cơm tấm sườn bì chả' for the full plate.

name: Banh Xeo
description: A large, crispy rice-flour crepe coloured with turmeric, filled with pork, prawns, mung beans and bean sprouts. The southern version is big, thin and bright yellow from turmeric and coconut milk.
how_to_eat: Wrap pieces in lettuce or mustard leaves with herbs and dip in sweet-sour fish sauce.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bánh xèo' at street stalls and family restaurants.

name: Goi Cuon
description: Fresh rolls of rice paper wrapped around rice vermicelli, shrimp, pork and herbs, served uncooked rather than fried. They are called gỏi cuốn in the south and nem cuốn in the north.
how_to_eat: Dip in hoisin-peanut sauce.
how_to_order: Ask for 'gỏi cuốn' at street stalls and restaurants.

name: Vietnamese Iced Coffee
description: Dark roast coffee dripped through a small metal phin filter onto sweetened condensed milk and poured over ice. It began as a colonial-era take on café au lait, using condensed milk because fresh milk was scarce.
how_to_eat: Stir the condensed milk up from the bottom before drinking.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cà phê sữa đá'; 'cà phê đen đá' is without milk.

name: Che
description: A family of sweet dessert soups and puddings made with beans, jellies, tapioca, fruit and coconut milk, served hot or over ice. Chè is made at home and also sold ready-made in cups.
how_to_eat: Stir the layers together and eat with a spoon.
how_to_order: Point at the toppings you want at a chè stall.

name: Hu Tieu
description: A noodle soup of Teochew origin with a pork-bone broth; hủ tiếu Mỹ Tho is topped with seafood, while hủ tiếu Nam Vang is Phnom Penh style. It is a southern breakfast dish.
how_to_eat: Season with lime, chilli and herbs; it can also be ordered dry with broth on the side.
how_to_order: Ask for 'hủ tiếu Mỹ Tho' or 'hủ tiếu Nam Vang', 'nước' (soup) or 'khô' (dry).

name: Ca Kho To
description: Catfish or snakehead braised in a clay pot with caramel sauce, fish sauce, pepper and garlic. The Mekong Delta is thought to be its birthplace.
how_to_eat: Eat with steamed rice and a sour soup.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cá kho tộ' at home-style rice restaurants.

name: Canh Chua
description: A hot and sour soup with tamarind, pineapple, tomato, okra and bean sprouts, usually with fish. It originates from the Mekong Delta.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice, often alongside cá kho tộ.
how_to_order: Ask for 'canh chua cá lóc' (with snakehead fish).

name: Bun Mam
description: Rice vermicelli in a pungent broth made from fermented fish, topped with seafood and pork. Of Cambodian origin, it is a specialty of the Mekong Delta.
how_to_eat: Add the raw vegetables and herbs served alongside.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bún mắm' at Mekong Delta noodle shops.

name: Banh Pia
description: A flaky Teochew-style pastry made with lard and filled with mung bean paste and durian, sometimes with salted egg yolk. It is a specialty of Sóc Trăng.
how_to_eat: Eat with hot tea.
how_to_order: Buy boxes of 'bánh pía' from bakeries in Sóc Trăng.
